name: Zero-carb carnivore

angle.text: Adherents eat only animal products to lose fat, hold muscle and, they say, clear skin and inflammation. Support comes mostly from self-reports, and dietetic bodies classify it as a fad diet.

summary: Animal foods only and no plants at all: popular online, supported mostly by self-reports, and classed as a fad diet by dietetic bodies.
note: Long-term safety has not been established; no large randomised trials exist.
currentQuick:
The zero-carb carnivore diet allows only animal foods such as meat, fish, eggs and sometimes dairy, with no plant foods and no added carbohydrate. Trace carbohydrate from animal sources is treated as acceptable. Shawn Baker and the Petersons helped popularise it from about 2017 to 2019.
Believers report better weight, digestion, mood and skin. The published evidence is limited to a 2021 self-selected survey, case reports and small series.
How it works: With almost no carbohydrate the body relies on fat and protein for energy, usually in ketosis. Advocates argue that excluding plant compounds such as lectins and oxalates helps some people and that animal foods supply bioavailable nutrients such as heme iron, B12 and preformed vitamin A.
Risks and caveats: Reported or discussed risks include lack of fibre, possible shortfalls of vitamin C and other micronutrients, sharply raised LDL cholesterol in some people, constipation, gout and kidney strain. The British Dietetic Association and Dietitians Australia classify it as a fad diet.
deepLead:
The carnivore diet, also called the zero-carb diet, is a high-protein, low-carbohydrate regimen in which adherents eat only animal products such as meat, dairy and eggs. Grokipedia describes the strict zero-carb version as the baseline, with no plants and no added carbohydrates, and trace carbohydrates from animal sources generally under 5 grams a day considered acceptable.
Orthopaedic surgeon Shawn Baker promoted the diet on social media from 2018, and Jordan and Mikhaila Peterson became prominent adherents. Supporters rely mainly on self-reported surveys and anecdotes; Grokipedia describes controlled long-term evidence as largely missing, while professional dietetic bodies regard the diet as a fad.

name: Ribeye and water carnivore

angle.text: Followers narrow carnivore eating to fatty beef and water, aiming for leanness, muscle and clearer skin through simplicity. It is an informal shorthand with no studies of its own.

summary: Strict carnivore eating built around fatty steak and water: a monotony-based protocol with no studies of its own.
note: Not described as a distinct named protocol in the sources; evidence applies only to the broader carnivore diet.
currentQuick:
Ribeye and water describes a very strict form of carnivore eating in which fatty steak is the main or only food. Grokipedia does not treat it as a separate named protocol, but notes carnivore advocates recommend fatty cuts such as ribeye, 80/20 ground beef and added tallow so that most calories come from fat.
Supporters describe simplicity and symptom relief. No study has tested it specifically.
How it works: Fat and protein supply energy with near-zero carbohydrate, typically in ketosis. Fatty cuts are favoured to avoid protein-heavy eating.
Risks and caveats: Concerns about the wider carnivore diet include fibre and micronutrient gaps, a documented scurvy case with mostly canned beef, raised LDL cholesterol, constipation, gout and kidney strain.
deepLead:
Ribeye and water is a shorthand for an extremely narrow carnivore diet built around fatty beef steaks and water. Grokipedia does not describe it as a distinct named protocol, but notes that carnivore advocates recommend fatty cuts such as ribeye, 80/20 ground beef and added tallow so that most calories come from fat rather than protein.
It belongs to the carnivore diet family, which allows only animal foods and excludes plants. Evidence for the family consists mainly of self-reports; dietetic bodies classify the diet as a fad diet.

name: Carnivore-ish / animal-based diet

chain: Clearer skin, leaner, more energy claimed
angle.text: Popularised by Paul Saladino, this looser carnivore diet is followed for clearer skin, better sleep and energy, and a leaner physique. Evidence is mostly testimonials; controlled research is limited.

summary: Paul Saladino's meat, organs, fruit, honey and raw dairy approach: a looser carnivore diet with plenty of testimonials and little controlled research.
note: Raw dairy carries food-safety concerns, and no trial has tested the diet as a whole.
currentQuick:
The animal-based diet centres on ruminant meat, organ meats, fish, eggs and often raw dairy, with limited fruit and honey for carbohydrate. It excludes vegetables, grains, legumes, nuts and seeds. It was popularised in the early 2020s by psychiatrist Paul Saladino as a refinement of the strict carnivore diet.
Proponents report better digestion, energy and mental clarity. Mainstream nutrition experts call it restrictive, and no clinical trial has tested the full pattern. Looksmax.org users post both enthusiastic essays and reports of poor sleep, fatigue and persistent acne after a year on it.
How it works: Advocates say animal foods are nutrient-dense and avoid plant defence chemicals such as lectins and oxalates, while fruit and honey add carbohydrate for energy. Short-term feeding research shows that an all-animal diet changes gut bacteria within days.
Risks and caveats: Concerns raised include missing fibre and plant nutrients, high saturated fat, and the safety of raw dairy. Saladino himself reported low energy, poor sleep and low testosterone on strict carnivore before adding fruit and honey, according to Grokipedia.
deepLead:
The animal-based diet emphasises nutrient-dense animal products such as meat, organ meats, fish, eggs and raw dairy, with limited low-toxicity fruits and honey, while excluding vegetables, grains, legumes, nuts and seeds. Wikipedia describes it as a looser variant of the carnivore diet, adding fruit, honey and raw dairy, and credits Paul Saladino with popularising the red-meat-based version.
Saladino, a psychiatrist, wrote The Carnivore Code in 2020, founded the organ-supplement company Heart & Soil that year, and later shifted from strict carnivore to an approach including fruit and honey, saying strict carnivore had left him with low energy, poor sleep and low testosterone, according to Grokipedia. Proponents claim improved digestion, mental clarity and chronic disease management, whereas mainstream nutrition experts regard the diet as restrictive with potential long-term risks.
On looksmax.org the diet is discussed both as an optimal human diet in long essays and as a disappointment by users reporting poor sleep, fatigue and acne after about a year.

name: Raw egg consumption

angle.text: Raw eggs are blended into shakes in strength-sports culture as an inexpensive protein and choline source for building muscle. Research reports lower protein absorption from raw than cooked eggs, and no appearance studies exist.

summary: Drinking raw eggs for protein and choline, Rocky-style: popular on forums, but health agencies flag Salmonella and research reports lower protein absorption than cooked eggs.
note: Salmonella risk is documented; avidin in raw egg white binds biotin.
currentQuick:
Some gym and looksmaxxing users drink or blend raw eggs for convenience, protein and choline, following the old strongman and Rocky Balboa image. Forum posts range from people reporting they drink a dozen or more at a time to threads arguing raw eggs are a meme.
Health authorities advise against eating raw eggs for vulnerable groups, and Wikipedia reports that egg protein is much less bioavailable raw than cooked.
How it works: Raw egg contributes protein, fat and choline. Raw egg white contains avidin, which binds biotin tightly, and cooking reduces this effect. Heat also kills Salmonella and makes the protein easier to digest.
Risks and caveats: Salmonella contamination of eggs is a recognised public health concern. Case-control research found raw eggs a leading risk factor for Salmonella Enteritidis infection, and raw egg allergy reactions have been reported even after tolerating cooked egg. Pasteurised eggs are sold as a lower-risk option.
deepLead:
Raw egg consumption means eating or drinking uncooked eggs, commonly blended into shakes. The practice is associated with strength-sports culture, including the image of Rocky Balboa drinking raw eggs, and appears on looksmax.org as a cheap protein and choline source.
Health sources describe two main concerns. Salmonella can contaminate eggs, either inside the egg from the hen or on a cracked shell, and heat destroys it. Raw egg white also contains avidin, which binds biotin, and Wikipedia reports that egg protein is about 51 percent bioavailable raw compared with roughly 91 percent cooked.
Forum users disagree about whether raw eggs are worth it, with some posting large daily intakes and others arguing cooked eggs deliver more protein and nutrients.

name: Liver / organ meats (beef liver)

chain: Vitamin A, B12 and iron intake
angle.text: Forum users eat beef liver as a nutrient-dense food for skin and vitality, citing its vitamin A, B12 and iron content. The nutrient content is well documented; trials on appearance have not been done.

summary: Beef liver is a genuinely nutrient-dense food that forums treat as a skin-and-vitality staple, with no trials on appearance and a documented vitamin A ceiling.
note: Very high in preformed vitamin A; health agencies advise limits on intake, especially in pregnancy.
currentQuick:
Beef liver is the organ of a cow, eaten in many cuisines. It is unusually rich in vitamin A, vitamin B12, riboflavin, copper and iron, and in looksmaxxing and ancestral-diet circles it is promoted as a whole-food alternative to multivitamins for skin, energy and general vitality.
No published human trial has tested liver consumption for skin, facial appearance or attractiveness. The nutritional content itself is well documented; the appearance claims are an extension of that content rather than something studied directly.
How it works: Proponents reason that nutrients concentrated in liver, especially preformed vitamin A, B vitamins and heme iron, support skin, hair and energy, so eating liver should improve them. The nutrient levels are measured facts; whether eating liver changes appearance in people who are not deficient has not been tested.
Risks and caveats: Liver contains preformed vitamin A, and reference sources note that a single serving can exceed the adult tolerable upper intake level of 3,000 micrograms per day. Excess preformed vitamin A is associated with headaches, liver damage, bone effects and, in pregnancy, harm to the fetus. Raw liver carries the food-safety concerns associated with any raw meat, and forum members dispute whether it should be eaten raw, frozen or cooked.
deepLead:
Liver is the organ most often meant by the term organ meats or offal in looksmaxxing and ancestral-diet communities. Beef liver in particular is promoted online as a very concentrated food, rich in preformed vitamin A, vitamin B12, riboflavin, copper and iron, and is described by some forum users as nature's multivitamin .
Reference sources confirm that liver is unusually nutrient-dense and that its vitamin A content is high enough that one slice of beef liver can exceed the adult tolerable upper intake level of 3,000 micrograms of preformed vitamin A per day . The same sources document vitamin A poisoning from liver, historically from polar bear, seal and husky livers, and advise caution in pregnancy .
No published trial has tested whether eating liver changes skin quality, facial appearance or attractiveness. The appearance claims on forums rest on the food's nutrient profile and on personal reports.

name: Desiccated organ supplements (beef organs capsules)

angle.text: Freeze-dried beef liver and organ capsules are taken as a convenient stand-in for eating organ meats, for skin, energy and general nutrition. They are marketed as a multivitamin alternative; no appearance trials exist.

summary: Freeze-dried beef liver and organ capsules marketed as a convenient 'nature's multivitamin', with no appearance trials behind them.
note: Liver-based products supply preformed vitamin A, for which an upper intake level exists; supplements are not regulated like drugs.
currentQuick:
Desiccated organ supplements are capsules or powders made from dried beef liver and sometimes other organs such as heart, kidney or spleen. They are sold as a way to get the nutrients of organ meats without cooking or tasting them, and are popular in ancestral-diet and looksmaxxing circles.
The underlying idea is that organ meats are nutrient-dense, which reference sources confirm for liver. No published trial was found testing these capsules for skin, hair, energy or appearance.
How it works: The capsules deliver the nutrients found in the source organ, mainly in liver preformed vitamin A, B12, riboflavin, iron and copper. Proponents say this supports skin and vitality; this has not been tested for the capsule products themselves.
Risks and caveats: Liver-derived products contain preformed vitamin A, for which health sources list a tolerable upper intake level of 3,000 micrograms per day for adults and advise limits in pregnancy. Dietary supplements are not approved as drugs, and content and quality vary by manufacturer.
deepLead:
Desiccated organ supplements, often sold as beef organ capsules, are dried and encapsulated preparations of animal organs, most commonly beef liver, sometimes combined with heart, kidney, spleen or other tissue. They are promoted in ancestral-diet communities as a convenient substitute for eating organ meats.
Liver, the main ingredient, is documented as a very rich source of preformed vitamin A, vitamin B12, riboflavin, iron and copper . Reference sources also document that excess preformed vitamin A can cause toxicity, including liver damage, bone effects and harm in pregnancy .
No published human study was found testing organ capsules for skin, appearance or general health outcomes, so claims about their benefits rest on the nutrient profile of the source organs and on user reports.

name: Bone marrow / bone broth

angle.text: Bone broth and marrow are consumed for collagen, with users hoping for firmer skin and healthier joints. They are long-standing foods; no published trials examine appearance.

summary: Slow-simmered bones and marrow, promoted for collagen and skin; popular as a food, with no published trials on appearance.
note: Reference sources state there is no scientific evidence for many of the health claims made for bone broth.
currentQuick:
Bone broth is stock made by simmering bones and connective tissue in water for a long time, and bone marrow is the fatty tissue inside long bones, eaten roasted or in soups. In wellness and looksmaxxing circles both are promoted for collagen, skin, joints and gut health.
Bone broth became a wellness trend in the early 2010s. Wikipedia reports there is no scientific evidence to support many of the claims made for it, and no published trial was found testing it for skin or appearance.
How it works: Simmering releases collagen from bones and connective tissue, which turns into gelatin. Proponents say eating this collagen supports skin and joints; how dietary collagen or gelatin is digested and whether it reaches skin in a meaningful way has not been established for broth specifically.
Risks and caveats: Broth and marrow are ordinary foods and are generally not regarded as risky for most people. Marrow is high in fat, and bones can concentrate contaminants in some preparations. Vertebral spinal marrow is banned for sale in some countries, including the UK, because of mad cow disease concerns.
deepLead:
Bone broth is a cooking liquid made by simmering bones, often with meat scraps, vegetables and herbs, for an extended period. During simmering, collagen in bones and connective tissue turns into gelatin, which thickens the liquid . Bone marrow is the edible tissue inside long bones, found in yellow and red forms, and has been eaten for a very long time .
Health claims about bone broth became popular in the early 2010s, helped by books such as Nourishing Broth (2014), and bone broth bars and delivery services grew in the United States . In looksmaxxing and wellness communities, broth is promoted for collagen, skin and joint support.
Wikipedia states that there is no scientific evidence to support many of the claims made for bone broth, citing NPR and Harvard Health . No published trial was found testing bone broth or marrow consumption for skin quality or appearance.

name: Beef tallow

chain: Used in cooking and on skin
angle.text: Beef tallow is used in ancestral-diet cooking and increasingly applied to the face as a moisturiser. Its use as cooking fat is long-standing; its skin and appearance effects are untested in trials.

summary: Rendered beef fat used for frying and, lately, as a face moisturiser; popular online, with no trials on its skin or appearance effects.
note: High in saturated fat and cholesterol; Wikipedia describes some seed-oil-versus-tallow claims as unscientific.
currentQuick:
Beef tallow is beef fat that has been rendered into a solid. It has long been used for frying, soap and candles, and has recently become popular with ancestral-diet and looksmaxxing communities, both as a cooking fat and as something to rub on the skin.
Its composition is well documented. No published human trial was found testing tallow for skin or appearance, and the claim that it is healthier than seed oils is described by Wikipedia as unscientific.
How it works: Tallow is almost pure fat, roughly half saturated and 42 percent monounsaturated. As a food it is a calorie-dense frying fat; applied to skin, fats generally act as occlusives that slow water loss. Whether tallow specifically offers skin benefits has not been tested.
Risks and caveats: As food, tallow is high in saturated fat and cholesterol, and older diet studies found saturated fats raise serum cholesterol. Topical use has no published safety data; moisturisers in general can cause contact dermatitis in some people.
deepLead:
Tallow is rendered beef, pork or mutton fat, made mostly of triglycerides. Beef tallow is about 50 percent saturated fat, 42 percent monounsaturated and 4 percent polyunsaturated, with roughly 109 mg of cholesterol per 100 g . It has long been used for frying, soap, candles and lubrication, and fast-food chains including McDonald's fried in tallow-based oil until around 1990 .
In recent years beef tallow has been promoted online as a healthier cooking fat than seed oils and as a skincare ingredient, a trend that has been associated with influencers and with US political figures . Wikipedia describes some of these claims as unscientific .
No published human trial was found testing tallow, eaten or applied, for skin condition or appearance. Dietary research on tallow is mostly older work on serum cholesterol and animal studies.

name: Tallow skincare

angle.text: Users apply whipped tallow balms to the face as a moisturiser, preferring a simple animal-fat product to conventional creams. It is popular online, and published trials on tallow itself are lacking.

summary: Rubbing rendered beef fat on the face as a moisturiser, popular online with no published trials on tallow itself.
note: No published safety or efficacy studies of tallow on skin; any moisturiser can cause contact dermatitis in some people.
currentQuick:
Tallow skincare means using rendered beef fat, alone or blended into balms, as a face and body moisturiser. It spread through ancestral-diet and wellness communities as part of a broader move toward traditional fats.
Supporters say tallow resembles the fats in human skin. No published trial was found testing tallow on skin, so those claims are untested.
How it works: Fats and oils applied to skin generally act as occlusives, forming a layer that slows water loss. Tallow is almost entirely fat and would be expected to do something similar, but no study has tested it, and its comedogenic or irritant potential has not been published.
Risks and caveats: There are no published safety studies for tallow as a skin product. Moisturisers in general can cause contact dermatitis in some users, and animal fats can go rancid or carry contaminants depending on how they are prepared.
deepLead:
Tallow skincare is the practice of applying rendered beef fat to the skin as a moisturiser, often in the form of a whipped balm. It is an application of beef tallow, a fat historically used in soap and candles .
Proponents online say tallow is a traditional, minimally processed moisturiser whose fatty acid profile resembles human skin oils. Moisturisers in general are described as products that protect and lubricate skin, largely by forming an occlusive layer that slows water loss .
No published human trial was found testing tallow on skin, and Wikipedia's articles on tallow and emollients do not discuss its skincare use .

name: Raw honey / bee pollen

angle.text: Raw honey and bee pollen are promoted for skin and testosterone. Honey has some wound-care evidence; the appearance benefits of both are described as unproven.

summary: Hive products promoted for skin and testosterone; honey has some wound-care evidence, bee pollen's benefits are described as unproven.
note: Bee pollen can trigger allergic reactions including anaphylaxis; honey is not recommended for infants under one year.
currentQuick:
Raw honey is honey that has not been heated or pasteurised, and bee pollen is the pollen pellets bees collect and store as food. In wellness and looksmaxxing circles both are promoted for skin, energy and testosterone.
Honey has preliminary evidence for some wound and burn dressings but none for appearance or hormones, and Wikipedia describes bee pollen's health benefits as unproven. No published trial was found testing either for skin appearance or testosterone in healthy people.
How it works: Honey is mostly fructose and glucose with some acids and aromatic compounds, and has antibacterial activity that varies between honeys. Bee pollen is a variable mix of sugars, protein, minerals, vitamins and fatty acids. How either would change skin or hormones has not been shown.
Risks and caveats: Bee pollen can cause allergic reactions in people allergic to pollen, ranging from hives to anaphylaxis, and may be contaminated with mycotoxins, pesticides or metals; it is not considered safe in pregnancy. Honey can carry Clostridium botulinum spores and is not recommended for infants under one year. The FDA has warned about bee pollen products adulterated with unapproved drugs.
deepLead:
Raw honey is honey taken from the hive and extracted, settled or strained without added heat, so it may retain some pollen and wax particles . Bee pollen is the ball of flower pollen that worker honeybees pack and use as the hive's main food, mixed with nectar and salivary secretions .
Both are promoted in wellness and looksmaxxing communities for skin, energy and testosterone. Honey is mostly fructose and glucose, with a pH averaging about 3.9, and is reported to have broad antibacterial activity . Bee pollen composition is variable, with about 40 to 60 percent simple sugars and 20 to 60 percent protein by one estimate .
For honey, preliminary evidence suggests faster healing of partial-thickness burns and moderate evidence for some post-operative wounds, while evidence for other uses is low quality or inconclusive . Wikipedia describes bee pollen's health benefits as yet unproven . No published trial was found testing either product for skin appearance or testosterone in healthy people.

name: Fruitarian diet

angle.text: Some in looksmaxxing communities eat only fruit in pursuit of clean, glowing skin and a lean body. There are no appearance trials, and case reports focus on nutritional problems.

summary: Eating only fruit for clean skin: no appearance trials exist, and case reports describe nutritional problems.
note: Fruit contains no vitamin B12; dietitians caution against long-term use.
currentQuick:
A fruitarian diet is based mainly or wholly on fruit, sometimes with nuts and seeds. Some people in appearance communities try it hoping for clearer skin and leanness.
No clinical trials have tested it for appearance. The published literature consists of case reports.
How it works: Followers say removing processed foods and animal products and eating water-rich, antioxidant-containing fruit improves skin. This mechanism has not been tested in studies.
Risks and caveats: Dietitians cite possible shortfalls of vitamin B12, protein, calcium, iron, zinc and vitamin D, high sugar load, and unsuitability for children and pregnant or nursing women. Case reports include reversible dementia and altered glucose control in type 1 diabetes.
deepLead:
A fruitarian diet is an eating pattern built primarily or entirely on fruit, sometimes with nuts and seeds, and without animal products. It is more restrictive than veganism or raw veganism, and practitioners differ on what counts as fruit and whether anything else is allowed. In looksmaxxing communities it is sometimes discussed as a route to "clean" skin and leanness.
Published research on the diet is limited to individual case reports. These describe a type 1 diabetes patient who adopted the diet for ideological reasons, a case of reversible dementia attributed to a strictly fruitarian diet, and a leukemia patient who combined a mostly fruitarian diet with long periodic fasts. No clinical trial has tested a fruitarian diet for skin or appearance outcomes.
Dietitians and health organisations cited in encyclopedic summaries advise against long-term fruit-only eating, citing the risk of deficiencies, particularly vitamin B12, and describe it as unsuitable for children and pregnant or nursing women.

name: Raw vegan diet

angle.text: Followers eat uncooked plant foods hoping for better skin, leanness and general health. Small studies cover nutrition status, none cover looks, and B12 intake is a recurring topic.

summary: Uncooked plant-only eating: small studies on nutrition, none on looks, and B12 is a recurring concern.
note: B12 and vitamin D shortfalls reported; child cases documented.
currentQuick:
A raw vegan diet is made of uncooked plant foods kept below roughly 40-49 degrees Celsius. People in appearance communities explore it for skin and leanness.
Research is limited to small observational studies and case reports; none examined appearance.
How it works: Proponents say heat destroys enzymes and nutrients. Dietetic sources say food enzymes are digested rather than doing digestive work and that cooking can improve availability of some nutrients.
Risks and caveats: Reported concerns include low B12, vitamin D and calories, and case reports of problems in children.
deepLead:
A raw vegan diet consists of uncooked plant foods, typically fruit, vegetables, nuts, seeds and sprouts, usually kept below roughly 40-49 degrees Celsius. It excludes animal products and, in many versions, most cooked or processed foods. It is discussed in appearance communities as a route to better skin, leanness and general health.
Studies are small and mostly observational. A study of long-term followers of a mostly raw vegan diet reported vitamin B12 status concerns, a cross-sectional study linked a low-calorie raw vegan diet and endurance exercise with low cardiometabolic risk factors, and case reports describe both athletic performance and complications. No trial has tested the diet for skin or facial appearance.
Dietetic sources note that cooking does not simply destroy nutrients, and that raw vegan diets may be low in vitamin B12, vitamin D and calories.

name: Vegan diet

angle.text: People adopt veganism for skin, leanness and, in anecdotal claims, lighter eye colour. Data are good for weight and cardiometabolic markers; appearance claims are mostly anecdotal.

summary: Plant-only eating: good data on weight and cardiometabolic markers, nothing on looks, and B12 must be supplemented.
note: B12 only from fortified foods or supplements.
currentQuick:
A vegan diet excludes all animal products. In appearance circles it is discussed for skin, leanness and sometimes eye colour.
Trials in type 2 diabetes and weight loss exist; no trials examine looks.
How it works: Vegan diets are higher in fibre and lower in saturated fat and shift gut microbiota; claimed skin effects are untested.
Risks and caveats: Main concern is vitamin B12, plus vitamin D, calcium, iodine, iron, zinc and omega-3. Major dietetic bodies say well-planned vegan diets suit all life stages.
deepLead:
A vegan diet excludes all animal-derived foods, including meat, fish, dairy, eggs and honey. The term was coined by Donald Watson and Dorothy Morgan in November 1944 when the Vegan Society was founded. People in appearance communities discuss it for skin, leanness and even eye colour, though most such claims are anecdotal.
Research is mostly observational and on health outcomes. A 2017 meta-analysis examined vegetarian and vegan diets against chronic disease and mortality outcomes, randomized trials of low-fat vegan diets in type 2 diabetes reported improved glycemic control and cardiovascular risk factors, and a meta-analysis of randomized trials examined weight change.
The Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics states that well-planned vegan diets are appropriate at all life stages, while a systematic review and other literature highlight nutrients needing attention, particularly vitamin B12.

name: Vegetarian / pescatarian

chain: Less meat, more plants and fish
angle.text: Vegetarian and pescatarian diets are used as reduced-meat options for skin, leanness and general health. Population data on health are decent; looks are not directly studied.

summary: Reduced-meat diets with decent population data on health but nothing on looks.
note: Some fish contain mercury; vegetarians should watch B12 and iron.
currentQuick:
Vegetarian diets exclude meat; pescatarian diets add fish and seafood. Both are common, moderate alternatives to omnivorous or vegan eating.
Studies are observational and focus on cancer, cardiovascular risk and nutrient status; none test appearance.
How it works: They shift intake toward plants and, for pescatarians, fish-derived omega-3. Any effect on skin or leanness is untested.
Risks and caveats: Nutrient status studies compare B12, iron and others across diets; some fish carry mercury and PCBs.
deepLead:
Vegetarian diets exclude meat, and pescatarian diets exclude meat but include fish and seafood; both may include eggs and dairy. The term pescetarian was coined in the UK in the late 1980s and about 3 percent of adults worldwide were estimated to follow this diet in 2017-2018. They are discussed in looksmaxxing contexts as reduced-meat options for skin, leanness and general health.
Research is mostly observational. A UK Biobank cohort and meta-analysis examined meat, vegetarian, pescatarian and fish-poultry diets and cancer risk, a Swiss population study linked these diets to cardiovascular risk factors, and studies of young people compared micronutrient status.

name: Mediterranean diet

angle.text: The Mediterranean pattern is used as a well-researched baseline diet for general health, skin and weight control. Cardiovascular evidence is strong; appearance is not directly studied.

summary: The best-researched diet pattern: strong cardiovascular data, but nothing on looks directly.
note: Appearance benefits are inferred from general health data.
currentQuick:
The Mediterranean diet is a plant-forward pattern built on olive oil, vegetables, legumes, fish and nuts. It is widely studied.
Trials and cohorts address cardiovascular outcomes and survival; skin and appearance outcomes have not been directly tested.
How it works: Proposed mechanisms include unsaturated fats, fibre and polyphenols, and effects on gut microbiota; this is explanatory rather than proven for looks.
Risks and caveats: Cost and nutrient gaps outside original cultural settings have been noted; moderate wine is part of the traditional pattern.
deepLead:
The Mediterranean diet is a traditional eating pattern of countries such as Greece, southern Italy and Spain. It emphasises vegetables, fruit, whole grains, legumes, nuts and extra-virgin olive oil, with moderate fish, poultry, eggs and dairy, low to moderate wine with meals, and limited red meat and sweets. Researcher Ancel Keys popularised the idea after the Seven Countries Study.
It is among the best-studied dietary patterns. Large cohort and trial evidence, including the PREDIMED trial in Spain and the Lyon Diet Heart Study, examined cardiovascular outcomes, and a Greek cohort linked adherence to survival. Appearance communities cite it as an evidence-based alternative to fad diets for skin and general health; direct trials on skin or looks were not identified.

name: Anti-inflammatory diet

angle.text: Users eat whole-food, low-processed diets to reduce facial puffiness and acne. Research targets inflammation markers and disease, not puffiness or acne directly.

summary: Whole-food, low-processed eating aimed at inflammation: research targets disease markers, not puffiness or acne.
note: Appearance claims are untested.
currentQuick:
An anti-inflammatory diet emphasises fish, berries, greens, olive oil and nuts and limits processed food and sugar. Appearance communities cite it for less puffiness and acne.
Studies look at inflammation markers and disease; none test facial outcomes.
How it works: The idea is that diet changes lower chronic low-grade inflammation, measured by markers such as CRP and IL-6.
Risks and caveats: Generally a conventional food pattern; individual conditions should be discussed with a clinician, as sources advise.
deepLead:
An anti-inflammatory diet is an eating pattern intended to lower chronic low-grade inflammation by emphasising whole foods rich in omega-3 fatty acids, polyphenols and fibre, while limiting processed foods, refined carbohydrates, added sugars and red and processed meat. The Mediterranean diet is commonly given as a model. In appearance communities it is cited for reducing puffiness and acne.
Research examines inflammation markers and diet indices, mostly for heart disease, bowel disease, depression and cognitive health. No trials were found on facial puffiness or acne with an anti-inflammatory diet as such.

name: Dairy-free for skin

angle.text: People avoid milk and sometimes other dairy to clear acne and, in some accounts, reduce facial puffiness. Observational studies link dairy to acne weakly; trials are lacking.

summary: Cutting milk to clear acne and puffiness: a popular idea backed by weak observational links, not by trials.
note: Evidence for milk restriction in acne was judged insufficient as of 2014.
currentQuick:
Dairy-free for skin means giving up milk, and sometimes all dairy, in the hope of fewer breakouts or a less puffy face. It is a common suggestion in skincare and looksmaxxing discussions.
Wikipedia's acne article describes weak observational evidence that dairy milk consumption is associated with more frequent and severe acne, and states that evidence was insufficient to recommend milk restriction as of 2014. No trial results are summarized for facial puffiness.
How it works: The proposed mechanism is that milk contains whey protein and hormones, including bovine IGF-1 and precursors of dihydrotestosterone, which could amplify insulin and IGF-1 signaling, androgen production, sebum output and comedone formation.
Risks and caveats: Dairy elimination has no safety issues identified in the sources used here. Milk is a source of nutrients, and people who remove it generally need to replace them from other foods.
deepLead:
Dairy-free for skin is the practice of avoiding milk, and sometimes other dairy products, to reduce acne and, in some online accounts, facial puffiness.
Wikipedia's acne article reports weak observational evidence that dairy milk consumption is positively associated with acne frequency and severity, and notes the proposed role of whey protein and hormones in milk. As of 2014, it says, the evidence was insufficient to recommend restricting milk for acne.

name: No-sugar / sugar-free lifestyle

chain: Lower glycation and blood sugar swings
angle.text: Users cut added sugar for clearer, younger-looking skin and a leaner body. Health guidelines support eating less sugar; skin-specific trials are thin.

summary: Avoiding added sugar for clearer, younger-looking skin: health guidelines back less sugar, but skin-specific trials are thin.
note: Sugar's effect on skin appearance is less studied than its general health effects.
currentQuick:
A no-sugar or sugar-free lifestyle means avoiding added and free sugars, often with the aim of reducing acne and slowing skin ageing through glycation. It is a frequent theme in skincare and looksmaxxing talk.
Public health bodies recommend limiting free sugars for general health, and Wikipedia reports that dermatologists suggest a diet low in simple sugars for acne. The sources reviewed do not discuss glycation or skin ageing.
How it works: For acne, the proposed route is through high blood sugar and insulin raising IGF-1 and androgen activity. Believers also invoke glycation, where sugars bind to proteins such as collagen, but that mechanism is not covered in the sources used here.
Risks and caveats: Cutting sugar is a mainstream dietary change. Extreme versions that remove whole food groups can affect nutrition.
deepLead:
A no-sugar or sugar-free lifestyle is an eating pattern that removes or strongly limits added sugars, adopted by some people to improve skin, among other aims.
The WHO recommends reducing free sugars to under 10 percent of energy intake and suggests below 5 percent as a further target. Wikipedia's acne article says dermatologists recommend a diet low in simple sugars to improve acne.

name: Gluten-free for skin

angle.text: Some people go gluten-free hoping to clear acne or skin inflammation. It is essential for celiac-linked rashes; no acne trials were found for people without such conditions.

summary: Going gluten-free for skin: essential for celiac-linked rashes, but no acne trials were found.
note: Gluten-free substitutes can lack iron and B vitamins and add sugar and fat.
currentQuick:
Gluten-free for skin is the idea that avoiding wheat, barley and rye clears acne or reduces inflammation. It circulates widely in wellness and looksmaxxing spaces.
A gluten-free diet is the established treatment for celiac disease and for dermatitis herpetiformis. Wikipedia's acne article does not discuss gluten, and no acne-specific trials were found in the sources reviewed.
How it works: Believers point to gluten-driven inflammation. In medical contexts, a gluten-free diet works for autoimmune gluten-triggered conditions such as celiac disease and the skin rash dermatitis herpetiformis.
Risks and caveats: Poorly chosen replacements can cause nutritional gaps such as lower iron and B vitamins and more sugar and saturated fat. Clinicians advise testing for celiac disease before starting the diet.
deepLead:
Gluten-free for skin refers to avoiding gluten-containing grains in the belief that it improves acne or skin inflammation.
A gluten-free diet is the only medically accepted treatment for celiac disease, and a cited review lists it as the only treatment for dermatitis herpetiformis. Wikipedia notes that non-coeliac gluten sensitivity may include eczema or rash. The gluten-free diet has been a fad diet since the early 2000s.

name: Low-sodium for face de-puffing

angle.text: Users lower salt intake to reduce perceived facial water retention and look more defined. Low sodium lowers blood pressure, but facial effects are unstudied in these sources.

summary: Cutting salt to slim a puffy face: low sodium lowers blood pressure, but facial effects are unstudied in these sources.
note: Very low sodium intake has been associated with increased risk in some analyses.
currentQuick:
This practice involves reducing salt intake in the belief that it reduces water retention and facial puffiness. It is a common tip in looksmaxxing communities for a leaner-looking face.
Health guidance supports lower sodium for blood pressure, but the sources reviewed do not discuss facial puffiness or edema. Wikipedia's acne article states evidence does not support a link between salt and acne.
How it works: Believers say sodium holds water in tissues. Wikipedia notes sodium is involved in the osmotic regulation of water content in body organs.
Risks and caveats: Wikipedia notes the association between sodium intake and cardiovascular disease or mortality may be U-shaped, with risk at both high and low intakes.
deepLead:
Low-sodium for face de-puffing is the practice of reducing salt intake to lessen perceived facial water retention.
The WHO recommends adults consume less than 2,000 mg of sodium a day, about 5 g of salt. Reducing sodium lowers blood pressure in adults and children, with a larger effect in hypertension. The sources reviewed do not address facial puffiness.
